text: 11 Lecture 11 11.1 Cayley-Hamilton theorem Proposition 11.1. Let A ∈ Mn×n(F ) and v be an eigenvector with eigenvalue λ. (i) For any f (x) ∈ F [x], f (A)(v) = f (λ)v thus f (λ) is an eigenvalue of f (A) and v is an eigenvector with eigenvalue f (λ). In particular, f (σ(A)) ⊂ σ(f (A)). (ii) If pA splits in F , then σ(f (A)) = f (σ(A)). Proof. (i) Ak(v) = Ak−1(A(v)) = λAk−1(v) = · · · = λkv. Suppose f (x) = anxn+· · ·+a0. Then f (A)v = (anAn + · · · + a0I)v = (anλn + · · · + a0)v = f (λ)v. (ii) Let µ ∈ σ(f (A)), i.e. f (A)v = µv for 0 ̸= v ∈ F n. Consider the polynomial f (x) − µ. Let E be a field extension of F such that f (x) − µ = (x − λ1) · · · (x − λm). Then 0 = (f (A) − µI)v = (A − λ1I) · · · (A − λmI)v. The matrix (A − λ1I) · · · (A − λmI) is singular since it maps a nonzero vector v to 0. So there must be 1 ≤ i ≤ m such that A − λiI is singular. Thus λi is an eigenvalue of A. However, since pA(x) splits in F , λi ∈ F and we have f (λi) − µ = 0 that is f (λi) = µ. Corollary 11.2. Let A ∈ Mn×n(F ) and f (x) ∈ F [x]. If f (A) = 0, then for any eigenvalue λ of A, we have f (λ) = 0. Example 11.3. If A2 = I, then the eigenvalue of A is either 1 or −1. If A2 = A then the eigenvalue of A is either 1 or 0. If Am = 0 then the eigenvalue of A is 0. Example 11.4. If pA does not splits in F , then there are A ∈ Mn×n(F ) and f ∈ F [x] such that f (σ(A)) ⊊ σ(f (A)). Let A = ( 0 1 −1 0 ) ∈ M2×2(R) and f (x) = x2. Then f (A) = (−1 0 0 −1 ). We have pA(x) = x2 + 1 and σ(A) = ∅ and σ(f (A)) = {−1}. Hence f (σ(A)) ⊊ σ(f (A)) = {−1}. Theorem 11.5 (Cayley-Hamilton theorem). Let A ∈ Mn×n(F ). Then pA(A) = 0. Remark 11.6. Wrong but not very wrong proof: pA(A) = det(AI − A) = det 0 = 0. This is wrong because plugging a matrix in det(xI − A) does not make sense and also pA(A) should be a matrix while in the above proof det 0 is a scalar. However, with some efforts, one can make this argument to work. See Chapter 6, Theorem 5 of Linear algebra and its applications by Lax. Proof when A is diagonalizable. Since A is diagonalizable, P −1AP = diag(λ1, . . . , λn). Then pA(A) = P pA(diag(λ1, . . . , λn))P −1 = P diag(pA(λ1), . . . , pA(λn))P −1 = 0 since λi are roots of pA. To deal with the case where A is not diagonalizable, we need the following theorem. 62 Theorem 11.7. Let A ∈ Mn×n(F ), pA splits as in F [x]. Then there exists P ∈ Mn×n(F ) invertible, such that P −1AP =      λ1 ∗ · · · ∗ 0 λ2 · · · ∗ ... ... . . . ... 0 0 · · · λn      where λ1, . . . , λn are the eigenvalues of A (with multiplicity). Proof. We prove the statement by induction on n. The base case n = 1 is trivial. Assume the statement is true for all matrices of size (n − 1) × (n − 1) whose char- acteristic polynomial splits in F . Since pA splits in F , A has at least one eigenvalue λ1 ∈ F . Choose a nonzero eigenvector v1 ∈ F n with Av1 = λ1v1. Extend {v1} to a basis (v1, v2, . . . , vn) of F n and let P1 = (v1 v2 · · · vn) be the change-of-basis matrix. In this basis the linear map A has matrix P −1 1 AP1 = (λ1 ∗ 0 B ) , where B ∈ M(n−1)×(n−1)(F ). By Proposition 8.14, pA(x) = (x − λ1)pB(x). Since pA(x) splits in F , we have pB(x) also splits in F . By the induction hypothesis there exists an Q ∈ M(n−1)×(n−1)(F ) invertible such that Q−1BQ is upper triangular with eigenvalues λ2, . . . , λn on the diagonal. Put P = P1 ( 1 0 0 Q ) . Then a direct block multiplication gives P −1AP =      λ1 ∗ · · · ∗ 0 λ2 · · · ∗ ... ... . . . ... 0 0 · · · λn      , which completes the induction and the proof. Lemma 11.8. If A =      λ1 ∗ · · · ∗ 0 λ2 · · · ∗ ... ... . . . ... 0 0 · · · λn      and B =      µ1 ∗ · · · ∗ 0 µ2 · · · ∗ ... ... . . . ... 0 0 · · · µn      then A + B =      λ1 + µ1 ∗ · · · ∗ 0 λ2 + µ2 · · · ∗ ... ... . . . ... 0 0 · · · λn + µn      63 and AB =      λ1µ1 ∗ · · · ∗ 0 λ2µ2 · · · ∗ ... ... . . . ... 0 0 · · · λnµn      . Note that ∗ may be different in different matrices. In particular, we have for any integer k ≥ 1 and f (x) ∈ F [x] Ak =      λk 1 ∗ · · · ∗ 0 λk 2 · · · ∗ ... ... . . . ... 0 0 · · · λk n      and f (A) =      f (λ1) ∗ · · · ∗ 0 f (λ2) · · · ∗ ... ... . . . ... 0 0 · · · f (λn)      . Proof. Directly verify using matrix addition and multiplication. Lemma 11.9 (Linear transformation given by an upper triangular matrix ). Let T : V → V be a linear transformation and β = (v1, . . . , vn) be a basis of V . If A = [T ] β β is an upper triangular matrix then T (Ej) ⊂ Ej for all j = 1, . . . , n where Ej = span(v1, . . . , vj). Moreover, if ajj = λj, then (T − λjid)(Ej) ⊂ Ej−1. Proof. Since A = [T ] β β is upper triangular, for any 1 ≤ j ≤ n, T (vj) = a1jv1+· · ·+ajjvj ∈ Ej. Thus T (Ej) ⊂ Ej. Since [T − λjid] β β = A − λjI is upper triangular, we have (T − λjid)(Ej−1) ⊂ Ej−1. On the other hand, (T −λjid)(vj) = a1jv1 +· · ·+ajjvj −λjvj = a1jv1 +· · ·+a(j−1)jvj−1 ∈ Ej−1. Since (T −λjid) maps a basis of Ej into Ej−1, we have (T −λjid)(Ej) ⊂ Ej−1. Proof. If pA(x) = (x−λ1) · · · (x−λn) splits, then by Theorem 11.7 there is P ∈ Mn×n(F ) invertible such that P −1AP =      λ1 ∗ · · · ∗ 0 λ2 · · · ∗ ... ... . . . ... 0 0 · · · λn      . Define the subspaces Ej = span(v1, v2, . . . , vj), where v1, v2, . . . , vn are the columns of P . 64 Take an arbitrary vector v ∈ F n = En. Then we have pA(A)v = (A − λ1I) · · · (A − λnI)v. Then we have (A − λnI)v ∈ En−1 (A − λn−1I)(A − λnI)v ∈ En−2 ... (A − λ2I) · · · (A − λnI)v ∈ E1. The last inclusion implies that (A − λ2I) · · · (A − λnI)v = cv1 for some c ∈ F . But (A − λ1I)v1 = 0, and hence 0 = (A − λ1I)(cv1) = (A − λ1I)(A − λ2I) · · · (A − λnI)v. Therefore, pA(A)v = 0 for all v ∈ F n, which means exactly that pA(A) = 0. If pA does not splits in F , then by Proposition 9.17, there is a field extension E of F such that pA(x) splits in E. We now view A as a matrix over E. Then the previous argument shows pA(A) = 0. Since pA is the same polynomial and pA(A) is the same matrix regardless of whether you think of them as over E or F , we finish the proof. 11.2 Minimal polynomial Theorem 11.10. There exists a unique polynomial such that (i) mA(x) is monic. (ii) mA(A) = 0 (iii) For any f (x) ∈ F [x] such that f (A) = 0, we have mA(x) | f (x). In fact, mA(x) is the monic nonzero polynomial with least degree such that mA(A) = 0. Proof. Consider the set IA = {f (x) ∈ F [x] : f (A) = 0}. By the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, the characteristic polynomial pA(x) = det(xI − A) ∈ IA, since pA(A) = 0. So IA ̸= {0}. Let mA be a nonzero polynomial in IA of least degree. We scale mA such that it is monic. Since mA ∈ IA, we have mA(A) = 0. For any f ∈ IA we have f (A) = 0. By Theorem 9.6, f (x) = mA(x)q(x) + r(x) where deg r < deg mA. Since 0 = f (A) = mA(A)q(A) + r(A) = r(A). We must have r = 0 since otherwise r ̸= 0 and we have r ∈ IA. deg r < deg mA. This contradicts mA has least degree in IA. Hence mA(x) | f (x). To show uniqueness, suppose that m1, m2 are two polynomials satisfying (i), (ii) and (iii). Then since m1(A) = 0, m2(x) | m1(x) by (iii) of m2(x). Since m2(A) = 0, m1(x) | m2(x) by (iii) of m1. Thus m1 = cm2 for some c ∈ F . Since m1 and m2 are both monic, we have m1 = m2. Definition 11.11. The polynomial mA(x) is called the minimal polynomial of A. 65 Example 11.12. A n × n Jordan block with diagonal λ is a matrix of the form Jn(λ) =          λ 1 0 · · · 0 0 0 λ 1 · · · 0 0 0 0 λ · · · 0 0 ... ... ... . . . ... ... 0 0 0 · · · λ 1 0 0 0 · · · 0 λ          ∈ Mn×n(F ). Then pJn(λ)(x) = (x − λ)n and by Propostion 11.13 mJn(λ)(x) = (x − λ)k for some 1 ≤ k ≤ n. Let N = Jn(λ) − λI. We have N (e1) = 0, N (ej) = ej−1 for any j = 2, . . . , n N 2(e1) = N 2(e2) = 0, N 2(ej) = ej−2 for any j = 3, . . . , n · · · N n−1(e1) = · · · = N n−1(en−1) = 0, N n−1(en) = e1 N n(e1) = · · · = N n(en) = 0. Thus mJn(λ)(x) = (x − λ)n. Proposition 11.13. If the characteristic polynomial pA(x) = (x − λ1) k1(x − λ2)k2 · · · (x − λm) km splits over F so the λi ∈ F are the distinct eigenvalues, then the minimal polynomial mA(x) has the same distinct linear factors, i.e. mA(x) = (x − λ1)l1(x − λ2) l2 · · · (x − λm)lm (5) with 1 ≤ li ≤ ki. In other words, every factor (x − λi) that appears in pA also appears in mA. Proof. By Theorem 11.7, there exists P ∈ Mn×n(F ) invertible such that P −1AP =      λ1 ∗ · · · ∗ 0 λ2 · · · ∗ ... ... . . . ... 0 0 · · · λn      . By Lemma 11.8, mA(A) = P      mA(λ1) ∗ · · · ∗ 0 mA(λ2) · · · ∗ ... ... . . . ... 0 0 · · · mA(λn)      P −1 = 0. Thus mA(λi) = 0 for all 1 ≤ i ≤ n. By Proposition 9.10, (x − λi) | mA(x) for any eigenvalue λi of A. 66 Theorem 11.14. Let A ∈ Mn×n(F ). Then A is diagonalizable over F if and only if the minimal polynomial mA(x) splits over F as a product of distinct linear factors, i.e. mA(x) = (x − λ1)(x − λ2) · · · (x − λm) where λ1, . . . , λm are distinct. In other words, l1 = · · · = lm = 1 in (5). Proof. “=⇒” If A is diagonalizable over F then there exists an invertible P with P −1AP = diag(λ1, . . . , λn), where each λj ∈ F . Let λ1, . . . , λm be the distinct eigenvalues of A. We define f (x) = (x−λ1) · · · (x−λm) ∈ F [x]. Then we have f (A) = P f (diag(λ1, . . . , λn))P −1 = 0. Thus mA(x) | f (x). By Proposition 11.13, we have f (x) | mA(x). Thus mA(x) = f (x). “⇐=” Conversely, suppose mA(x) = (x−λ1)(x−λ2) · · · (x−λm) with distinct λi ∈ F . We define pi(x) = (x−λ1) · · · (x−λi−1)(x−λi+1) · · · (x−λn). By Lagrange interpolation theorem (Homework 9 Problem 4), 1 = m∑ i=1 cipi(x), ci = 1 (λi − λ1) · · · (λi − λi−1)(λi − λi+1) · · · (λi − λn) . Substituting A for x gives a decomposition of the identity matrix as a sum of matrices I = m∑ i=1 Pi, Pi := cipi(A). For any v ∈ F n we have v = ∑m i=1 Piv. For each 1 ≤ i ≤ m, (A − λiI)Piv = ci(A − λiI)pi(A)v = cimA(A)v = 0v = 0. Thus Piv ∈ E(λi, A). Hence F n decomposes as a direct sum of eigenspaces F n = E(λ1, A) + · · · + E(λm, A) = E(λ1, A) ⊕ · · · ⊕ E(λm, A). Therefore A is diagonalizable over F by Theorem 10.11. Example 11.15. If A2 = A then A is diagonalizable with eigenvalue 1 or 0. This is because f (x) = x2 − x ∈ IA. Then mA(x) | f (x). Since f (x) splits as distinct linear factors, mA(x) splits as distinct linear factors. Similarly, if A2 = I, then A is diagonalizable with eigenvalue 1 or −1. 67
